SAGRADX collapses the boundaries between the sacredness of private and public life through the interactions of the personal, Queer, Latinx and institutional. Across painting, durational performance, photography, sculpture and installation, Perry Picasshoe searches for enduring and ephemeral ways to capture, preserve and present what is held sacred.

The Riverside Art Museum welcomes the community to celebrate the art and stories of California Collectives: Asian American Moderns 1924-1965 during Free First Sunday on October 4, 2026. From noon to 3pm audiences will be immersed in the art and culture of the exhibition through art, music, and hands-on-art-making activities. Following the Community Day, the museum will partner with The Center for Social Justice & Civil Liberties to present an exhibition-related panel discussion – the first time the museum has so intentionally collaborated with The Center for Social Justice on programming.

Long before their names faded from memory, Asian American artists were winning prizes, headlining exhibitions, and helping to shape modern American art. Join Tracy Fisher, Director of the Center for Social Justice & Civil Liberties and Drs. Shannon Vittoria and ShiPu Wang, curators of LACMA’s California Collectives: Asian American Moderns, 1924-1965 (on view at the Riverside Art Museum through November 1, 2026), as they bring to light this forgotten story from a period of U.S. history when discriminatory laws and “Yellow Peril” stereotypes cast immigrant and U.S.-born Asians as perpetual outsiders. Artists of Asian descent refused to be defined by xenophobia, as they exhibited alongside America’s canonical artists while organizing their own art collectives—welcoming friends of all backgrounds—and staging ambitious shows from San Francisco to Little Tokyo. Through their art, they told their own stories and claimed their place in American life. Discover a legacy of creativity, community, and belonging that’s finally getting the recognition it deserves.
